title: Semantic Interoperability Across Securities, Cash and Accounting Ledgers
subtitle: Identifiers, ISO 20022 events, authoritative state and financial consistency
abstract: Interoperability is often framed as moving a token from Chain A to Chain B. Financial systems require a more demanding outcome: independent institutions must agree which obligation changed, which party became entitled, when money discharged the debt and which ledger entry represents the legally relevant event. This report proposes a semantic interoperability model across token contracts, custodians, payment rails and accounting systems.

evidence.heading: Interlinking existing rails need not rely on a new shared ledger
evidence.body: The BIS Project Nexus blueprint standardizes connections between domestic instant payment systems, while Meridian explores synchronization between central bank RTGS and other infrastructure. Agorá explores a shared platform with modular national and bank roles. These examples offer competing coordination architectures rather than a single universal blockchain bridge. The design should select infrastructure based on required rights and finality, not the availability of a cross-chain protocol.

evidence.heading: Standards convey structure but do not settle legal obligations
evidence.body: ISO 20022 payment messages can describe participants, amounts, purpose and processing states, but data format consistency alone does not guarantee that a token transfer constitutes irrevocable payment or legal asset delivery. A financial event also requires instrument identity, governing terms and the authority establishing the completion status. The BIS/CPMI report highlights how token arrangements change institutional processes and responsibilities, not merely message transports.

evidence.heading: External audit depends on event populations
evidence.body: An institution might have perfectly consistent token balances while its bank's payment account contains a missing refund or its custodian records unacknowledged securities. The FSB's assessment underscores the operational risk of complex tokenized interconnections. Synchronizing message streams cannot reconstruct legally unrecorded claims without independent source evidence. TSP-01's RPI should therefore treat completeness and provenance as explicit interface guarantees.

architecture.heading: Define a canonical economic-event envelope
architecture.body: Use an EconomicEventID and correlate contract/obligation ID, legal asset identifier, payer, payee, beneficial owner, currency, amount, effective time, settlement instructions, instruction status and finality authority. Carry source message and proof references separately from normalized interpretations. State transitions should be versioned and signed when they change rights; not every web or chain webhook has authority to alter the obligation.

architecture.heading: Map to systems with different semantics
architecture.body: ISO 20022 pacs messages may express interbank customer credit transfer or settlement instructions, and camt messages can report statements and notifications; a smart-contract Transfer log changes token balances; a bank core ledger records assets and liabilities; a custodian register maintains legal securities positions. A mapping table must document which system owns each field and which message is merely evidence. Unrecognized or ambiguous status codes should become exceptions rather than inferred success.

architecture.heading: Idempotency and causal ordering
architecture.body: Guarantee each economic action has a unique idempotency key, causal parent if it is a correction, replay nonce and settled/failed state version. Deliveries may be duplicated, reordered or delayed across bank and blockchain systems. Do not double count a provisional notification as a settled payment, and do not overwrite a previously final state without an explicit compensating business event.

architecture.heading: Verify end-to-end state rather than bridge messages
architecture.body: A useful protocol output is not simply token A burned and token B minted. It is a signed evidence package identifying the original claim, acceptance conditions, independent finality proof, completed owner or payee entitlement and corresponding accounting position. Privacy may require private proofs or permissioned access to details; transparent message identifiers should not expose sensitive investor or bank data.

case.title: One USD 75,000 event across four institutions
case.setup: A buyer makes a USD 75,000 approved payment to an assigned creditor while a related tokenized receivable is retired. The payment network, token ledger, rights registry and general ledger are independently operated.
rows: Distinct provisional and final status messages
Payable discharged; cash and claim entries
Balancing postings and external bank statement
case.formula: Event consistency requires one economic event ID linked to distinct system records. A mapping is complete only when all required financial-state assertions are present, not when each interface returned HTTP 200.
case.interpretation: A token burn cannot settle the buyer's payable if the bank payment failed. Equally, a bank payment can be final before the token registry is corrected, creating a controlled operational exception.

risks: 'Accepted' interpreted as irrevocably settled across two incompatible rails.
Explicit state translation tables and finality authority.
Two payment notifications trigger two claim cancellations.
Economic-event idempotency, monotonic status and replay detection.
Cross-ledger proof publishes full investor identities and transaction descriptions.
Selective disclosure and segregated off-chain confidential records.
tests: Round-trip a sample transfer from business event to ISO 20022-like message, token event and journal with field-level provenance.
Reorder and duplicate messages, including a final status before an earlier provisional notification, and prove consistent outcomes.
Compare shared-ledger versus interlinked-rail designs under a bank-operator outage and partial asset settlement.
conclusion: RPI should be a semantic protocol for financial obligations and independently attested outcomes. A cryptographic bridge is only one possible transport component, not a substitute for legal entitlement, rail finality or audit reconstruction.

title: Bridge, Gateway and Synchronization Designs: Trust and Failure Boundaries
subtitle: Cross-chain token movement versus legally effective capital-market interoperability
abstract: A DLT bridge may transfer a token representation between networks, but its security depends on custody, validators, proof verification, upgrade governance and recovery processes. A financial institution may instead use a gateway to preserve the authoritative asset registry and synchronize events with an external bank rail. This report compares three design families and defines the evidence required for safe capital-market interoperation.

evidence.heading: Multiple topologies are being tested
evidence.body: Project Agorá explores a shared programmable wholesale infrastructure; Meridian and Meridian FX demonstrate coordination among existing payment systems and external assets; Nexus develops standardized interlinks among instant payment systems. These architectures have different trust and governance boundaries. Financial institutions should not conclude that any one architecture is universally superior based only on a successful proof of concept.

evidence.heading: Token duplication can create distinct legal claims
evidence.body: A lock-and-mint bridge may create a wrapped token on a destination chain while the source asset remains locked in a contract. That arrangement produces reliance on the bridge custodian, proof mechanisms and a redemption path. The destination token is not automatically legally identical to the underlying security or an issuer-authorized representation. The FSB's concerns about complexity and interconnections are material where the bridge itself becomes an additional counterparty.

evidence.heading: Bank rail gateways have different failure semantics
evidence.body: When a banking interface is used, payments may become final under RTGS or bank clearing rules even if the DLT system remains unavailable. Synchronization operators are designed to coordinate such systems but require trusted status messages and operational fallback. An asynchronous bridge between financial obligations can reduce reconciliation lag without promising atomic cancellation of an already-final external payment.

architecture.heading: Lock/mint and burn/release
architecture.body: Source tokens are immobilized and destination representations created after verification; redemption burns or locks destination units and releases source assets. Under a simplified invariant, source assets locked must be sufficient for outstanding wrapped claims, subject to ratios and fees. The bridge must define which verifier can approve release, proof finality depth, emergency pause and failure recovery. Source-chain reorgs or validator collusion can violate assumptions.

architecture.heading: Institutional gateway and authoritative registry
architecture.body: A gateway may record a change in wallet control while keeping the legal holder ledger and custody system authoritative in one jurisdiction or network. This avoids creating competing wrapped supply but introduces a control-plane dependency on the issuer, registrar and network operator. The gateway must authenticate parties, enforce eligibility and prevent duplicated instructions across APIs and chain events.

architecture.heading: Synchronization operator for multi-rail delivery
architecture.body: A coordinator can reserve or condition asset and money legs on separately administered ledgers. Instead of inventing a new mirrored asset, it asks each system for authenticated hold/accept/finality evidence and triggers release under predetermined rules. It must document the last reversible point, the effect of operator insolvency, and what happens when one leg has become final but the other is pending.

architecture.heading: Security assurance and operability
architecture.body: Evaluate upgrade and key control, validator diversity, recovery duration, ledger finality, replay resistance, force-unwind policy, privacy, source-of-truth hierarchy and data retention. A bridge can be technically audited yet economically unsafe if its wrapped token exceeds eligible underlying assets. Maintain externally sourced backing and liability checks.

case.title: Synthetic transfer of 1,000 tokenized units between ledgers
case.setup: An issuer-authorized asset representation has 1,000 transferable units on Ledger A. An intermediary proposes to make them tradable on Ledger B. The legal terms prohibit duplicating outstanding beneficial claims.
rows: Conservation assumes 1:1 ratio and uncompromised bridge
1,000 source records move to a controlled destination register
200 unbacked claims, even if both ledgers internally balance
case.formula: Simplified bridge coverage = eligible locked source assets − outstanding redeemable wrapped claims. In fault case: 1,000 − 1,200 = −200 units. Negative coverage requires a controlled response, not a cosmetic price adjustment.
case.interpretation: The same UX promise—'move token across networks'—can create very different custody and legal risks. Financial product design should begin with the authorized holder and asset backing record.

risks: Unauthenticated wrapped mint creates unbacked economic claims.
Independent collateral/supply monitoring and threshold approval.
A legally valid owner change remains unacknowledged by the token venue.
Durable transaction queue and explicit pending status.
Investors rely on intermediary for redemption of locked source tokens.
Legal segregation, replacement operator and claims waterfall.
tests: Fault-inject unauthorized 20% wrapped supply increase and require early detection by independent asset coverage checks.
Simulate a source-chain reorganization after destination mint; evaluate the needed proof delay or rollback policy.
Compare bridge, gateway and synchronization against legality, completion time, liquidity lock-up and worst-case holder loss.
conclusion: DLT interoperability should preserve financial rights and auditable capital flows rather than privilege token mobility. RPI should explicitly compare trust topologies and provide a recovery protocol whenever infrastructure boundaries make atomicity impossible.
